title: Teaching on Purpose #8: Communicating Meaning
author: Adam Kohlbeck
summary: Adam Kohlbeck's eighth installment of the 'Teaching on Purpose' series focuses on how teachers communicate meaning -- not just information -- by making explicit connections between what students are learning and why it matters. The piece draws on the Chiltern Learning Trust's six core purposes framework and features Yamina Bibi's work on intellectual preparation: the idea that a student's capacity to receive new learning is determined not just by their prior content knowledge but by their sense of the purpose of the learning and their belief that it is connected to something worth understanding. Kohlbeck argues that meaning-communication is not motivational window-dressing but a cognitive prerequisite: students who understand why they are learning something are better able to form the schemas that make learning stick. The piece includes classroom protocols for meaning communication, including explicit purpose statements, connection-to-prior-knowledge rituals, and what Kohlbeck calls 'so that' teaching -- every objective stated not as a skill but as a tool for achieving something the student already cares about.
points: * Meaning communication is not motivational window-dressing but a cognitive prerequisite: students who understand why they are learning something form better schemas and retain more than students who do not. * Yamina Bibi's intellectual preparation framework argues that a student's capacity to receive new learning is determined in part by their sense of the purpose of the learning and their belief that it connects to something worth understanding. * The Chiltern Learning Trust's six core purposes framework provides teachers with a taxonomy for meaning-making: every lesson can be grounded in at least one of the six purposes, giving both teacher and student a richer vocabulary for the 'why.' * 'So that' teaching reframes lesson objectives: instead of 'students will be able to identify the main argument,' the objective becomes 'students will be able to identify the main argument so that they can evaluate whether the evidence actually supports it.' * Prior knowledge connection rituals -- explicit bridge-building from new content to what students already know and care about -- are meaning-communication tools that activate schema and reduce cognitive load simultaneously.
quotes: Yamina Bibi's work on intellectual preparation changed how I think about lesson openings. The question is not just 'do students have the prior knowledge they need?' It is 'do students believe that what they're about to learn is worth their attention?' Those are different cognitive conditions, and both need to be met for deep learning to occur.

The Chiltern Learning Trust's six core purposes are not a motivational poster. They are a design framework. When I know which purpose a lesson is serving, I can communicate that purpose explicitly, and that explicit communication changes the student's cognitive orientation toward the content.

Every lesson objective can be written as a 'so that' statement. 'Students will identify the main argument' is a task. 'Students will identify the main argument so that they can evaluate whether the author has actually proven their case' is a meaning. The difference in the student's engagement is not small.

Prior knowledge connection is not warm-up. It is cognitive preparation. It activates the schemas that new information needs to attach to. A lesson that skips this step is a lesson that starts cold, and cold starts are a reliable way to produce surface-level, quickly forgotten learning.

What I have learned from watching teachers who communicate meaning well is that they never assume meaning is obvious. They state it. They connect it. They return to it. They treat the 'why' as a load-bearing element of the lesson, not as a nice-to-have introduction.
